stories.title: 20th Anniversary of Rights of Nature
stories.summary: Twenty years ago, a small Pennsylvania borough passed the first law in the Western world giving nature enforceable legal rights. Tamaqua's ordinance — born from residents fighting toxic waste dumping in an old coal pit — has since inspired over 60 U.S. communities and 35 countries to recognize the rights of nature.
stories.extended_summary: In 1972, a law professor asked a wild question in a journal article: "Should trees have standing?" Thirty-four years later, a working-class Pennsylvania borough answered yes. Tamaqua had spent a century as a sacrifice zone — first for coal mining, then as a dumping ground for fly ash and sewage sludge. When residents learned hundreds of truckloads of toxic waste were headed for the pit bordering their town, organizer Cathy Morelli ran for council and helped pass an ordinance declaring that "natural communities and ecosystems shall be considered to be 'persons'" under law. It was the first time in Western legal history that nature had enforceable rights. Twenty years later, that idea has spread to over 60 local governments and tribal nations in the U.S. and more than 35 countries. Morelli's cancer clusters didn't matter to the corporations. Now, legally, the ecosystem does.

On Fiji's Kioa Island, Lotomau Fiafia stands with his grandson where the shoreline used to be when he was young. The court's unanimous ruling — that countries have a legal obligation to limit greenhouse gas emissions — was the culmination of a years-long campaign launched by law students in Vanuatu. For Indigenous communities, climate change isn't measured in degrees or dollars. It's a spiritual and cultural injury. Now, for the first time, international law says that injury counts.

stories.title: Why Great Plains Ranchers Are Setting Fire to Their Own Land
stories.summary: Ranchers across the Great Plains are setting their own grasslands on fire — on purpose. These carefully controlled burns clear out invasive cedar and dead fuel, revitalizing prairie grass for cattle and making catastrophic wildfires far less likely to spread. The Coffey family burned nearly 22,000 acres this year alone.
stories.extended_summary: Smoke hangs thick over southern Oklahoma's Arbuckle Mountains as flames move through prairie grass toward a stand of invasive red cedars. To most people, it looks like a disaster. To Chuck and Seth Coffey, it's the best tool they have. The father-son ranchers run 30,000 contiguous acres at Double C Cattle Company, and this year they burned close to 22,000 acres — including their neighbors' land. The logic is simple: burn in late winter, and by the time spring winds arrive that can turn a spark into a conflagration, there's no fuel left to feed it. Prescribed burns also revitalize native prairie plants, which means more food for cattle. "When wildfire does happen, we've already treated much of the landscape," Seth says. "We're dealing with it on our terms."

stories.title: At Dartmouth, Jewish and Middle Eastern Studies refuse to stay apart
stories.summary: After Oct. 7, Dartmouth student Jackson Weinstein stopped talking about the conflict — it was costing him friends. Then he enrolled in "Difficult Conversations on the Middle East," a course where students learn mindfulness and emotional regulation before ever debating the war.
stories.extended_summary: Jackson Weinstein used to be "extremely outspoken" about Israel on Dartmouth's campus. By sophomore year, he'd gone quiet. "It felt like I was losing friends and just making things harder for myself," said Weinstein, now a senior. Then he signed up for "Difficult Conversations on the Middle East," a course jointly offered by Dartmouth's Middle East and Jewish Studies departments in response to campus divisions nationwide. For the first several weeks, students didn't touch the conflict at all — they studied groupthink, mindfulness, emotional regulation, and academic freedom. Only in week five did they wade into Palestinian armed resistance, women's rights, genocide accusations, and colonialism. "In the first class, students come in with this idea of, 'How do I win the debate?'" said professor Jonathan Smolin. The course is teaching them something harder: how to actually listen.

stories.title: Crews Move Thousands of Mussels Before Pen Dam Removal
stories.summary: Snorkel-clad crews spent days in Michigan's Huron River relocating about 3,000 freshwater mussels before the Pen Dam is removed. The mussels can move, just not fast enough to escape the sediment a demolition would stir up.
stories.extended_summary: Wearing masks, snorkels, gloves, and knee pads, teams spent days turning over rocks in the Huron River — searching for animals that couldn't save themselves. They found about 3,000 freshwater mussels and moved them from slow water along the banks to the faster-flowing center of the channel, out of reach of sediment that will churn when Ypsilanti's Peninsular Paper Dam comes down. 'They can move, but they usually can't move fast enough,' says Paul Steen of the Huron River Watershed Council. Built in 1867 and classified high-hazard, the dam is slated for removal as early as 2027 after a $7.5 million federal grant.
